title: Ὡς τε λέοντα
titleEn: The Lion Among the Trojans — Iliad 5.111–216
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Sthenelus draws the arrow from Diomedes’ shoulder, and Diomedes prays to Athena to let him kill the man who hit him. She gives him back his father’s untrembling might, lifts the haze from his eyes so that he can tell gods from men, and warns him to strike no god but Aphrodite, should she come. Diomedes goes back among the front-fighters with three times his old strength, like a lion that a shepherd has only grazed as it leaps the sheep-yard. He kills Astynous and Hyperon, then Abas and Polyidus, whose father could read dreams but not his own sons’ fate, and then Xanthus and Thoon, whose old father leaves no heir, so that distant kin share out his property. He drags two sons of Priam from their chariot as a lion breaks the neck of a cow. Aeneas sees the slaughter and goes to find Pandarus, and asks him where his bow and his fame have gone. Pandarus answers that he has already hit Diomedes in the shoulder and Menelaus too, and neither fell, so a god must be shielding the man. He has no chariot here, for he would not take his father’s advice and bring his horses, and he swears to burn his useless bow if he ever gets home.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, Σθένελος δὲ καθ’ ἵππων ἆλτο χαμᾶζε,
πὰρ δὲ στὰς βέλος ὠκὺ διαμπερὲς ἐξέρυσ’ ὤμου·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, Sthenelos de kath’ hippōn alto chamaze,
par de stas belos ōky diamperes exerys’ ōmou·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and Sthenelus from the horses leapt to the ground,
and standing beside him the swift shaft right through drew out of the shoulder;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Sthenelus leapt from his horses to the ground, and standing beside him drew the swift shaft right through and out of the shoulder;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη ‘so he spoke’ closes Diomedes’ speech to Sthenelus in the last part, and Sthenelus now does as he was told. καθ’ ἵππων is κατὰ ἵππων with the κατά cut short, ‘down from the horses’ (the horses stand for the chariot they draw), and πὰρ δὲ στάς is παρὰ δὲ στάς, ‘and standing beside’. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’. ἐξέρυσ’ is ἐξέρυσε, ‘drew out’, with διαμπερές ‘right through’ and the genitive ὤμου ‘out of the shoulder’.

sentences.t: αἷμα δ’ ἀνηκόντιζε διὰ στρεπτοῖο χιτῶνος.
sentences.tr: haima d’ anēkontize dia streptoio chitōnos.
sentences.l: and the blood was spurting up through the twisted tunic.
sentences.i: and the blood was spurting up through the twisted tunic.
sentences.n: αἷμα ‘blood’ is the subject of ἀνηκόντιζε, the imperfect of ἀνακοντίζω ‘spurt up’ (from ἄκων ‘javelin’, so ‘shoot up like a javelin’), and διά takes the genitive στρεπτοῖο χιτῶνος, ‘through the twisted tunic’. What στρεπτός means here is not settled: ‘twisted’ (woven of twisted thread) or ‘pliant’. The blood comes from the wound in his shoulder.

sentences.t: δὴ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἠρᾶτο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: dē tot’ epeit’ ērato boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Then at that moment he prayed, Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Then Diomedes, good at the war-cry, prayed:
sentences.n: δὴ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ piles up three words for ‘then’ (‘then indeed, at that moment, next’) to mark the moment of the prayer. ἠρᾶτο is the imperfect middle of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet of Diomedes (and of Menelaus). His prayer runs to line 120 and has the usual shape: the god is called, reminded of past help, and asked.

sentences.t: κλῦθί μευ αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη,
sentences.tr: klythi meu aigiochoio Dios tekos Atrytōnē,
sentences.l: “Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone,
sentences.i: “Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone,
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and it takes the genitive μευ (= μου) ‘me’. αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος ‘child of aegis-bearing Zeus’ is a stock address to Athena (the meaning of αἰγίοχος is disputed), and Ἀτρυτώνη is a title of hers that is left untranslated because its meaning is not known. The same line opens Penelope’s prayer to Athena (Odyssey 4.762) and Odysseus’ (6.324).

sentences.t:
εἴ ποτέ μοι καὶ πατρὶ φίλα φρονέουσα παρέστης
δηΐῳ ἐν πολέμῳ, νῦν αὖτ’ ἐμὲ φῖλαι Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr:
ei pote moi kai patri phila phroneousa parestēs
dēïōi en polemōi, nyn aut’ eme philai Athēnē·
sentences.l:
if ever, for me and for my father, thinking kindly, you stood by
in hostile war, now again love me, Athena;
sentences.i: if ever you stood by me and by my father with kindly thoughts in hostile war, now again show your love to me, Athena;
sentences.n: εἴ ποτε ‘if ever’ opens the reminder of past help, and νῦν αὖτ’ ‘now again’ turns to the request. μοι καὶ πατρί is ‘for me and for my father’ (Tydeus). φίλα is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘kindly’, with φρονέουσα, the feminine participle of φρονέω ‘think’, which agrees with the ‘you’ of παρέστης (the aorist of παρίστημι ‘stand by’). δηΐῳ is the epic form of δήϊος ‘hostile’. φῖλαι is taken as an aorist imperative of φιλέω ‘love, befriend’, ‘show love to me’; its ending is not the usual one and the exact formation is uncertain. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’.

sentences.t:
δὸς δέ τέ μ’ ἄνδρα ἑλεῖν καὶ ἐς ὁρμὴν ἔγχεος ἐλθεῖν
ὅς μ’ ἔβαλε φθάμενος καὶ ἐπεύχεται, οὐδέ μέ φησι
δηρὸν ἔτ’ ὄψεσθαι λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
dos de te m’ andra helein kai es hormēn encheos elthein
hos m’ ebale phthamenos kai epeuchetai, oude me phēsi
dēron et’ opsesthai lampron phaos ēelioio.
sentences.l:
and grant me the man to take, and into the spear’s rush to come,
who struck me, getting in first, and vaunts, and says that I shall not
long yet see the bright light of the sun.”
sentences.i: and grant that I may kill the man and come within the rush of my spear, he who struck me by getting in first and cries out in triumph, and says that I shall not go on seeing the bright light of the sun for long.”
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘give, grant’, followed by two infinitives: ἑλεῖν, ‘take’, which in battle means ‘kill’, and ἐλθεῖν ‘come’. ὁρμὴν ἔγχεος is ‘the rush of the spear’, the distance a thrown or thrust spear covers. ὅς ‘who’ goes with ἄνδρα, the man who wounded him (Pandarus, not named here). φθάμενος is the aorist participle of φθάνω, ‘getting in first’, and ἐπεύχεται ‘vaunts’ (εὔχομαι with ἐπί) is what Pandarus did at 5.102–106. φησι takes the infinitive ὄψεσθαι, ‘says that I shall see’, with οὐδέ making it negative; ‘to see the light of the sun’ means ‘to be alive’. The closing quotation mark is Diomedes’ prayer ending.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος· τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’ euchomenos· tou d’ eklye Pallas Athēnē,
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and Pallas Athena heard him,
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him,
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος is the same phrase as at 106, but there it followed a boast and meant ‘so he declared’; here εὐχόμενος is ‘praying’, because εὔχομαι means both. τοῦ is the pronoun ‘him’, in the genitive because ἔκλυε, the aorist of κλύω, takes the genitive of the one heard. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is the stock name.

sentences.t: γυῖα δ’ ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρά, πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν·
sentences.tr: guia d’ ethēken elaphra, podas kai cheiras hyperthen·
sentences.l: and made his limbs light, his feet and his hands above;
sentences.i: and made his limbs light, his feet and his hands and the limbs above them;
sentences.n: γυῖα ‘limbs’ is the object of ἔθηκεν ‘made’, with ἐλαφρά ‘light’ saying what they were made. πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν is literally ‘feet and hands above’; it is taken as ‘his feet and his hands and the limbs above them’, but the exact sense of ὕπερθεν here is not settled.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and standing close by, winged words she spoke to him:
sentences.i: Standing close beside him, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱσταμένη (the feminine participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, here Athena) set the scene, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘she spoke winged words to him’ is the stock introduction to a speech; προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. Her speech to Diomedes runs to line 132.

sentences.t: θαρσῶν νῦν Διόμηδες ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr: tharsōn nyn Diomēdes epi Trōessi machesthai·
sentences.l: “Taking courage now, Diomedes, to fight against the Trojans;
sentences.i: “Take courage now, Diomedes, and fight against the Trojans;
sentences.n: θαρσῶν is the present participle of θαρσέω ‘take courage’ (Attic θαρρέω), and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is an infinitive; the two together stand for a command, ‘take courage and fight’. Διόμηδες is the vocative of Διομήδης, and ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι with the dative is ‘against the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
ἐν γάρ τοι στήθεσσι μένος πατρώϊον ἧκα
ἄτρομον, οἷον ἔχεσκε σακέσπαλος ἱππότα Τυδεύς·
sentences.tr:
en gar toi stēthessi menos patrōïon hēka
atromon, hoion echeske sakespalos hippota Tydeus·
sentences.l:
for into your breast your father’s might I have put,
untrembling, such as he used to have, shield-shaking Tydeus the horseman;
sentences.i: for I have put into your breast your father’s might, untrembling, such as shield-shaking Tydeus the horseman used to have;
sentences.n: ἐν … ἧκα, with the preposition cut off from its verb, is ‘I have put into’ (ἧκα is the aorist of ἵημι), with ἐν γάρ τοι στήθεσσι ‘for in your breast’ (τοι = σοι). μένος ‘might’ is the object; πατρώϊον ‘your father’s’ and ἄτρομον ‘untrembling’ (ἀ- + τρέμω) agree with it, and οἷον is ‘such as’. ἔχεσκε is an iterative imperfect, ‘used to have’. σακέσπαλος, ‘shield-shaking’, is from σάκος ‘shield’ and πάλλω ‘shake, brandish’, but the second part is not certain. ἱππότα ‘horseman’ is a nominative in -α, as in Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ. Tydeus is Diomedes’ father, the model of the might Athena says she has given him.

sentences.t:
ἀχλὺν δ’ αὖ τοι ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ἕλον ἣ πρὶν ἐπῆεν,
ὄφρ’ εὖ γιγνώσκῃς ἠμὲν θεὸν ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρα.
sentences.tr:
achlyn d’ au toi ap’ ophthalmōn helon hē prin epēen,
ophr’ eu gignōskēis ēmen theon ēde kai andra.
sentences.l:
and the haze besides from your eyes I took away, which before was upon them,
so that well you may know both god and man.
sentences.i: and I have taken away from your eyes the haze that lay on them before, so that you may clearly recognise both god and man.
sentences.n: ἀχλύν ‘haze’ is the object of ἕλον ‘I took away’ (the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’), ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ‘from your eyes’; the relative ἥ is feminine, agreeing with ἀχλύν, and ἐπῆεν is the imperfect of ἔπειμι ‘be upon’, ‘lay on them’. With the haze gone Diomedes can see the gods who are on the field. ὄφρ’ (ὄφρα) with the subjunctive γιγνώσκῃς gives purpose, ‘so that you may recognise’, and ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ καί is ‘both … and’.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν αἴ κε θεὸς πειρώμενος ἐνθάδ’ ἵκηται
μή τι σύ γ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς ἀντικρὺ μάχεσθαι
τοῖς ἄλλοις·
sentences.tr:
tō nyn ai ke theos peirōmenos enthad’ hikētai
mē ti sy g’ athanatoisi theois antikry machesthai
tois allois·
sentences.i: So now, if any god comes here to make trial of you, do not fight head-on with any of the other immortal gods;
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore, so’. αἴ κε is εἴ κε ‘if’ and takes the subjunctive ἵκηται ‘should come’ (the simple verb, for Attic ἀφίκηται), and θεὸς πειρώμενος is ‘a god making trial’, with the one tried left unsaid. μή τι σύ γ’ … μάχεσθαι is a prohibition made with the infinitive, ‘do not you, at any rate, fight’; ἀντικρύ is ‘straight on, head-on’, and τοῖς ἄλλοις ‘the others’ sets the rest of the gods against Aphrodite, who comes next.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ εἴ κε Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη
ἔλθῃσ’ ἐς πόλεμον, τήν γ’ οὐτάμεν ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr:
atar ei ke Dios thygatēr Aphroditē
elthēis’ es polemon, tēn g’ outamen oxeï chalkōi.
sentences.l:
but if the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite,
should come into the war, her at least wound with the sharp bronze.”
sentences.i: But if Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, should come into the war, wound her at least with the sharp bronze.”
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ ‘but’ marks the exception. Διὸς θυγάτηρ Ἀφροδίτη is ‘Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus’; ἔλθῃσ’ is ἔλθῃσι, the aorist subjunctive of ἔρχομαι, so εἴ κε … ἔλθῃσ’ is ‘if … should come’. οὐτάμεν is οὐτάμεναι, the aorist infinitive of οὐτάω ‘wound’, doing the work of a command, and τήν γ’ ‘her at least’ is put first for emphasis. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with the sharp bronze’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
sentences.tr: hē men ar’ hōs eipous’ apebē glaukōpis Athēnē,
sentences.l: She, indeed, then so having spoken went away, gleaming-eyed Athena,
sentences.i: So she spoke, and gleaming-eyed Athena went away,
sentences.n: ἣ μέν is the pronoun ‘she’ with μέν, set against Τυδεΐδης δέ in the next line. ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is ‘having so spoken’ (the aorist participle, feminine, of λέγω), and ἀπέβη ‘went away’, with γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη ‘gleaming-eyed Athena’ the stock epithet for her; ἄρ’ is ἄρα.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδης δ’ ἐξαῦτις ἰὼν προμάχοισιν ἐμίχθη
καὶ πρίν περ θυμῷ μεμαὼς Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Tydeïdēs d’ exautis iōn promachoisin emichthē
kai prin per thymōi memaōs Trōessi machesthai·
sentences.l:
and the son of Tydeus, going again among the front-fighters, mingled,
even before, though eager in his heart to fight the Trojans;
sentences.i: and the son of Tydeus went again to mingle with the foremost fighters, though even before he had been eager at heart to fight the Trojans;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’ (Diomedes). ἐξαῦτις ἰών is ‘going again’, and ἐμίχθη (the aorist passive of μίγνυμι) ‘mingled with’, here ‘joined’, with the dative προμάχοισιν ‘the foremost fighters’ (πρόμαχοι, from πρό ‘in front’ and μάχομαι ‘fight’). καὶ πρίν περ θυμῷ μεμαώς is ‘though even before he was eager at heart’: περ makes it concessive, and μεμαώς is the perfect participle of μάω, ‘eager’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε μιν τρὶς τόσσον ἕλεν μένος ὥς τε λέοντα
ὅν ῥά τε ποιμὴν ἀγρῷ ἐπ’ εἰροπόκοις ὀΐεσσι
χραύσῃ μέν τ’ αὐλῆς ὑπεράλμενον οὐδὲ δαμάσσῃ·
sentences.tr:
dē tote min tris tosson helen menos hōs te leonta
hon rha te poimēn agrōi ep’ eiropokois oïessi
chrausēi men t’ aulēs hyperalmenon oude damassēi·
sentences.i: Then thrice as much might seized him, like a lion that a shepherd on the farm, tending his fleecy sheep, wounds lightly as it leaps over the yard, but does not overcome;
sentences.n: A simile begins at ὥς τε λέοντα ‘like a lion’ and runs to line 142. μένος ‘might’ is the subject of ἕλεν ‘took hold of’ (the aorist of αἱρέω), with τρὶς τόσσον ‘three times as much’. ὅν ῥά τε … χραύσῃ … οὐδὲ δαμάσσῃ are subjunctives of a general case (‘whichever lion a shepherd may graze’), χραύω meaning ‘graze, wound slightly’. ἀγρῷ is ‘on the farm’ and ἐπ’ εἰροπόκοις ὀΐεσσι ‘over his fleecy sheep’, in his charge (εἰροπόκος ‘wool-bearing’). ὑπεράλμενον is the aorist participle of ὑπεράλλομαι ‘leap over’, with the genitive αὐλῆς.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μέν τε σθένος ὦρσεν, ἔπειτα δέ τ’ οὐ προσαμύνει,
ἀλλὰ κατὰ σταθμοὺς δύεται, τὰ δ’ ἐρῆμα φοβεῖται·
sentences.tr:
tou men te sthenos ōrsen, epeita de t’ ou prosamynei,
alla kata stathmous dyetai, ta d’ erēma phobeitai·
sentences.l:
its strength he rouses, and then does not come to defend,
but into the steadings he slips down, and the deserted ones are terrified;
sentences.i: he rouses its strength and then does not come to the defence, but slips away into the steadings, while the abandoned ones are terrified;
sentences.n: ὦρσεν (the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’) is a gnomic aorist, a timeless statement in a simile, and is rendered in the present: the shepherd ‘rouses’ the lion’s strength (τοῦ is the lion’s) by wounding it, and then does not come to the defence (προσαμύνει ‘ward off, help’; no object is given). κατὰ σταθμοὺς δύεται is ‘slips down into the steadings’ (δύομαι ‘sink into, enter’; σταθμός is a farm building), and τὰ δ’ ἐρῆμα φοβεῖται is ‘the abandoned ones are terrified’: τά is a pronoun, ἐρῆμα ‘deserted, left alone’, and a plural neuter subject takes a singular verb. The abandoned ones are the sheep.

sentences.t:
αἳ μέν τ’ ἀγχιστῖναι ἐπ’ ἀλλήλῃσι κέχυνται,
αὐτὰρ ὃ ἐμμεμαὼς βαθέης ἐξάλλεται αὐλῆς·
sentences.tr:
hai men t’ anchistinai ep’ allēlēisi kechyntai,
autar ho emmemaōs batheēs exalletai aulēs·
sentences.l:
and these, close together, are heaped one upon another,
but he, eager, leaps out of the deep yard;
sentences.i: while the sheep huddle close together, heaped one upon another, he in his eagerness leaps out of the deep yard;
sentences.n: αἳ μέν are the sheep (feminine plural ‘these’); ἀγχιστῖναι ‘close together’ is a rare word taken from ἄγχι ‘near’, and κέχυνται is the perfect passive of χέω ‘pour’, ‘have been poured’ in a heap. αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’ is the lion; ἐμμεμαώς is the perfect participle of ἐμμάω, ‘be eager’, and ἐξάλλεται ‘leaps out’ takes the genitive βαθέης αὐλῆς ‘out of the deep yard’.

sentences.t: ὣς μεμαὼς Τρώεσσι μίγη κρατερὸς Διομήδης.
sentences.tr: hōs memaōs Trōessi migē krateros Diomēdēs.
sentences.l: so, eager, he mingled with the Trojans, strong Diomedes.
sentences.i: So, in his eagerness, strong Diomedes mingled with the Trojans.
sentences.n: ὣς … μεμαώς closes the simile: ‘so, eager’. μίγη is ἐμίγη, the aorist passive of μίγνυμι without the augment (‘mingled’, as ἐμίχθη in line 134), and Τρώεσσι ‘with the Trojans’ is dative. κρατερὸς Διομήδης is the stock name and epithet.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἕλεν Ἀστύνοον καὶ Ὑπείρονα ποιμένα λαῶν,
τὸν μὲν ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο βαλὼν χαλκήρεϊ δουρί,
sentences.tr:
enth’ helen Astynoon kai Hypeirona poimena laōn,
ton men hyper mazoio balōn chalkēreï douri,
sentences.l:
There he took Astynous and Hyperon, shepherd of the people,
the one, above the nipple having struck him, with a bronze-fitted spear,
sentences.i: There he killed Astynous and Hyperon, shepherd of the people, hitting the one above the nipple with his bronze-fitted spear,
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there, then’. ἕλεν ‘took’ is from αἱρέω, which in battle regularly means ‘kill’ (the following lines say how). The names are Ἀστύνοον and Ὑπείρονα; ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock title for a leader, and being singular it is usually taken with the nearer name, Ὑπείρονα. τὸν μέν ‘the one’ is the first of the two, and the other comes in τὸν δ’ ἕτερον in the next unit. ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο is ‘above the nipple’ (μαζός ‘breast, nipple’), βαλών is ‘having hit’, and χαλκήρεϊ δουρί ‘with a bronze-fitted spear’ is dative of means.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἕτερον ξίφεϊ μεγάλῳ κληῗδα παρ’ ὦμον
πλῆξ’, ἀπὸ δ’ αὐχένος ὦμον ἐέργαθεν ἠδ’ ἀπὸ νώτου.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ heteron xipheï megalōi klēïda par’ ōmon
plēx’, apo d’ auchenos ōmon eergathen ēd’ apo nōtou.
sentences.l:
and the other with a great sword on the collar-bone beside the shoulder
struck, and from the neck the shoulder he cut away, and from the back.
sentences.i: and the other he struck with his great sword on the collar-bone beside the shoulder, and cut the shoulder away from the neck and from the back.
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἕτερον ‘and the other’ is the second of the two men, struck (πλῆξ’, the elided πλῆξε, the aorist of πλήσσω without the augment) with his great sword (ξίφεϊ μεγάλῳ, the epic dative of ξίφος) ‘on the collar-bone beside the shoulder’: κληΐς, usually ‘key, bar’, is here the collar-bone. ἐέργαθεν is an aorist of ἐέργω ‘shut off, keep apart’, in a rare form with -αθ-, and its object ὦμον ‘shoulder’ is cut ἀπ’ αὐχένος … ἠδ’ ἀπὸ νώτου ‘from the neck and from the back’ (ἠδ’ is ἠδέ ‘and’).

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἔασ’, ὃ δ’ Ἄβαντα μετῴχετο καὶ Πολύειδον
υἱέας Εὐρυδάμαντος ὀνειροπόλοιο γέροντος·
sentences.tr:
tous men eas’, ho d’ Abanta metōicheto kai Polyeidon
huieas Eurydamantos oneiropoloio gerontos·
sentences.l:
Those he left, and he went after Abas and Polyidus,
sons of Eurydamas, the dream-interpreting old man;
sentences.i: He left those two, and went after Abas and Polyidus, sons of Eurydamas, the old interpreter of dreams;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν ‘those’ are the two just killed; ἔασ’ is ἔασε, ‘left’ (the aorist of ἐάω). ὃ δ’ ‘but he’ is Diomedes, and μετῴχετο is the imperfect of μετοίχομαι ‘go after’. Ἄβαντα and Πολύειδον are accusatives, and υἱέας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός ‘son’, in apposition. In Εὐρυδάμαντος ὀνειροπόλοιο γέροντος, ὀνειροπόλος means ‘interpreter of dreams’ (from ὄνειρος ‘dream’), in the epic genitive -οιο, and γέροντος is ‘old man’.

sentences.t:
τοῖς οὐκ ἐρχομένοις ὃ γέρων ἐκρίνατ’ ὀνείρους,
ἀλλά σφεας κρατερὸς Διομήδης ἐξενάριξε·
sentences.tr:
tois ouk erchomenois ho gerōn ekrinat’ oneirous,
alla spheas krateros Diomēdēs exenarixe·
sentences.l:
for them, as they set out, the old man did not interpret the dreams,
but them strong Diomedes despoiled;
sentences.i: The old man did not interpret the dreams for them as they set out, but strong Diomedes killed them and stripped them of their armour;
sentences.n: τοῖς … ἐρχομένοις is ‘for them as they set out’, a dative participle; ἐκρίνατ’ is ἐκρίνατο, the aorist middle of κρίνω ‘judge, sort’, which with ὀνείρους ‘dreams’ means ‘interpret’. The point is that the old man’s skill did not save his sons. σφεας is the epic accusative ‘them’, and ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of armour’.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ μετὰ Ξάνθόν τε Θόωνά τε Φαίνοπος υἷε
ἄμφω τηλυγέτω·
sentences.tr:
bē de meta Xanthon te Thoōna te Phainopos huie
amphō tēlygetō·
sentences.l:
And he went after Xanthus and Thoon, the two sons of Phaenops,
both late-born;
sentences.i: Then he went after Xanthus and Thoon, the two sons of Phaenops, both of them late-born;
sentences.n: βῆ δὲ μετά is ‘and he went after’. Ξάνθον and Θόωνα (Xanthus and Thoon) are accusatives, Φαίνοπος υἷε ‘the two sons of Phaenops’ is a dual (υἷε), and ἄμφω τηλυγέτω ‘both late-born’ is dual too. τηλύγετος ‘late-born’ is the traditional sense; its origin is not known.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ τείρετο γήραϊ λυγρῷ,
υἱὸν δ’ οὐ τέκετ’ ἄλλον ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι λιπέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ho de teireto gēraï lygrōi,
huion d’ ou teket’ allon epi kteatessi lipesthai.
sentences.l:
and he was being worn down by grievous old age,
and had begotten no other son to be left behind over his possessions.
sentences.i: He, their father, was being worn down by grievous old age, and had fathered no other son to be left behind in charge of his possessions.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is the father, Phaenops. τείρετο is the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down’, and γήραϊ λυγρῷ is ‘by grievous old age’ (γῆρας, dative γήραϊ). τέκετ’ is τέκετο, the aorist middle of τίκτω, used of a father, ‘begot’; ἄλλον ‘other’ goes with υἱόν. ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι λιπέσθαι is ‘to be left behind over his possessions’ (κτέατα ‘possessions’, epic dative -εσσι; λιπέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of λείπω, here with a passive sense), an infinitive of purpose.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε τοὺς ἐνάριζε, φίλον δ’ ἐξαίνυτο θυμὸν
ἀμφοτέρω,
sentences.tr:
enth’ ho ge tous enarize, philon d’ exainyto thymon
amphoterō,
sentences.l:
There he was despoiling them, and the dear life he took away
from them both,
sentences.i: There he stripped them of their armour and took the dear life from them both,
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε is ‘there he’ (Diomedes) and τοὺς ‘them’ the two sons. ἐνάριζε is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω ‘strip of armour’ (the verb can also mean ‘kill’), and ἐξαίνυτο the imperfect middle of ἐξαίνυμαι ‘take away’: θυμός of the life that leaves the body is ‘life’. ἀμφοτέρω is the dual ‘both’, in apposition to τούς.

sentences.t:
πατέρι δὲ γόον καὶ κήδεα λυγρὰ
λεῖπ’, ἐπεὶ οὐ ζώοντε μάχης ἐκνοστήσαντε
δέξατο·
sentences.tr:
pateri de goon kai kēdea lygra
leip’, epei ou zōonte machēs eknostēsante
dexato·
sentences.i: and he left their father lament and grievous sorrows, since he did not receive them back alive, home from the battle;
sentences.n: πατέρι δέ is the dative ‘to the father’, and γόον καὶ κήδεα λυγρά ‘lament and grievous sorrows’ is what Diomedes left him (λεῖπ’ is λεῖπε, the imperfect without the augment). ἐπεὶ οὐ … δέξατο is ‘since he did not receive’ them: δέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι without the augment, and its object, the two sons, is not stated but described by two dual participles, ζώοντε ‘living’ and ἐκνοστήσαντε ‘having come home out of’ (ἐκνοστέω), with the genitive μάχης ‘from the battle’.

sentences.t: χηρωσταὶ δὲ διὰ κτῆσιν δατέοντο.
sentences.tr: chērōstai de dia ktēsin dateonto.
sentences.l: and distant kinsmen divided up the property.
sentences.i: and distant kinsmen divided up the property.
sentences.n: χηρωσταί is a rare word, understood as ‘distant kinsmen’ who inherit when there is no direct heir. διὰ … δατέοντο is ‘divided up among themselves’ (διά cut off from its verb; δατέοντο is the imperfect middle of δατέομαι ‘divide’), and κτῆσιν ‘property’ is the object.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ υἷας Πριάμοιο δύω λάβε Δαρδανίδαο
εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ἐόντας Ἐχέμμονά τε Χρομίον τε.
sentences.tr:
enth’ huias Priamoio dyō labe Dardanidao
ein heni diphrōi eontas Echemmona te Chromion te.
sentences.l:
There two sons of Priam, the Dardanid, he caught,
being in one chariot, Echemmon and Chromius.
sentences.i: Then he caught two sons of Priam, descendant of Dardanus, as they were in one chariot, Echemmon and Chromius.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there, then’; υἷας is the epic accusative plural of υἱός ‘sons’. Πριάμοιο … Δαρδανίδαο is ‘of Priam, the Dardanid’ (Δαρδανίδης is a patronymic from Dardanus, the ancestor of Troy’s kings; both genitives are epic forms in -οιο, -αο). δύω is ‘two’, λάβε ‘took hold of, caught’ (the aorist of λαμβάνω), εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ‘in one chariot’ (εἰν = ἐν) with ἐόντας (= ὄντας) ‘being’. Ἐχέμμονα and Χρομίον follow in apposition.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ λέων ἐν βουσὶ θορὼν ἐξ αὐχένα ἄξῃ
πόρτιος ἠὲ βοὸς ξύλοχον κάτα βοσκομενάων,
sentences.tr:
hōs de leōn en bousi thorōn ex auchena axēi
portios ēe boos xylochon kata boskomenaōn,
sentences.l:
And as a lion among cattle, having leapt, may break the neck
of a heifer or of a cow, down in the thicket, as they graze,
sentences.i: And as a lion, leaping among the cattle, snaps the neck of a heifer or a cow as they graze in the thicket,
sentences.n: ὡς δὲ λέων opens a second simile. θορών is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’; ἐξ … ἄξῃ, with the preposition cut off from its verb, is ‘break out’, here ‘snap’, the aorist subjunctive of ἄγνυμι in a general statement, with αὐχένα ‘neck’ as object. πόρτιος ἠὲ βοός is ‘of a heifer or a cow’, and βοσκομενάων (the epic genitive plural feminine of βοσκόμενος ‘grazing’) is ‘of those grazing’, so one out of the herd; ξύλοχον κάτα is κατὰ ξύλοχον, the preposition put after its noun, ‘down in the thicket’.

sentences.t:
ὣς τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ἐξ ἵππων Τυδέος υἱὸς
βῆσε κακῶς ἀέκοντας, ἔπειτα δὲ τεύχε’ ἐσύλα·
sentences.tr:
hōs tous amphoterous ex hippōn Tydeos huios
bēse kakōs aekontas, epeita de teuche’ esyla·
sentences.l:
so those two both from the horses the son of Tydeus
made go down, roughly, unwilling, and then their armour he was stripping;
sentences.i: so the son of Tydeus forced both of them down from their horses, roughly, against their will, and then stripped their armour;
sentences.n: ὣς … closes the simile. τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ‘both of them’ is the object of βῆσε, the causative aorist of βαίνω (ἔβησε ‘made go’), so ‘made them go down’ ἐξ ἵππων ‘from their horses’ (the horses stand for the chariot). κακῶς ‘roughly’ and ἀέκοντας ‘unwilling’ (ἀέκων = ἄκων) describe it. Τυδέος υἱός ‘the son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ἐσύλα the imperfect of συλάω ‘strip’.

sentences.t: ἵππους δ’ οἷς ἑτάροισι δίδου μετὰ νῆας ἐλαύνειν.
sentences.tr: hippous d’ hois hetaroisi didou meta nēas elaunein.
sentences.l: and the horses to his own companions he gave to drive to the ships.
sentences.i: and the horses he gave to his companions to drive to the ships.
sentences.n: ἵππους δ’ is ‘but the horses’; οἷς is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’, with ἑτάροισι ‘companions’. δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι ‘give’, and ἐλαύνειν ‘to drive’ the infinitive of purpose, μετὰ νῆας ‘to the ships’ (μετά with the accusative).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἴδεν Αἰνείας ἀλαπάζοντα στίχας ἀνδρῶν,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἄν τε μάχην καὶ ἀνὰ κλόνον ἐγχειάων
Πάνδαρον ἀντίθεον διζήμενος εἴ που ἐφεύροι·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ iden Aineias alapazonta stichas andrōn,
bē d’ imen an te machēn kai ana klonon encheiaōn
Pandaron antitheon dizēmenos ei pou epheuroi·
sentences.i: Aeneas saw him laying waste the ranks of men, and set out through the battle and the turmoil of spears, looking for godlike Pandarus in case he might find him somewhere;
sentences.n: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’ (Diomedes); ἴδεν is εἶδεν without the augment. ἀλαπάζοντα (the present participle of ἀλαπάζω ‘lay waste’) takes στίχας ἀνδρῶν ‘the ranks of men’. βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is ‘set out to go’, and ἄν (= ἀνά, cut short) … ἀνά with the accusative is ‘up through’ the battle and the κλόνον ἐγχειάων ‘turmoil of spears’ (κλόνος ‘confusion’, ἐγχείη ‘spear’). διζήμενος ‘seeking’ (from δίζημαι) governs Πάνδαρον, with ἀντίθεον ‘godlike’ agreeing, and εἴ που ἐφεύροι is ‘in case he might somewhere find him’ (the optative of ἐφευρίσκω).

sentences.t:
εὗρε Λυκάονος υἱὸν ἀμύμονά τε κρατερόν τε,
στῆ δὲ πρόσθ’ αὐτοῖο ἔπος τέ μιν ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
heure Lykaonos huion amymona te krateron te,
stē de prosth’ autoio epos te min antion ēuda·
sentences.l:
He found the son of Lycaon, both blameless and strong,
and stood before him and a word to him face to face spoke:
sentences.i: He found the blameless and strong son of Lycaon, and stood in front of him and spoke to him face to face:
sentences.n: εὗρε ‘found’ (the aorist of εὑρίσκω) has Aeneas as its subject; Λυκάονος υἱὸν is Pandarus, described by ἀμύμονά τε κρατερόν τε, ‘both blameless and strong’ (the sense of ἀμύμων is not known for certain; ‘blameless’ is the usual explanation). στῆ is ἔστη ‘stood’, πρόσθ’ αὐτοῖο ‘before him’ (πρόσθε with an epic genitive), and ἔπος τέ μιν ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘and spoke a word to him face to face’, ηὔδα being the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. His words follow to line 178.

sentences.t:
Πάνδαρε ποῦ τοι τόξον ἰδὲ πτερόεντες ὀϊστοὶ
καὶ κλέος;
sentences.tr:
Pandare pou toi toxon ide pteroentes oïstoi
kai kleos;
sentences.l:
“Pandarus, where are your bow and the winged arrows
and your fame?
sentences.i: “Pandarus, where are your bow and your winged arrows and your fame?
sentences.n: Πάνδαρε is the vocative. ποῦ τοι τόξον … is ‘where is your bow?’ with the verb ‘is’ left out (τοι = σοι), and ἰδέ is the epic form of ἠδέ ‘and’. πτερόεντες ὀϊστοί are ‘winged arrows’ (ὀϊστός ‘arrow’), and κλέος ‘fame’ is a third thing asked after: the bow, the arrows and the fame that comes from them.

sentences.t:
ᾧ οὔ τίς τοι ἐρίζεται ἐνθάδε γ’ ἀνήρ,
οὐδέ τις ἐν Λυκίῃ σέο γ’ εὔχεται εἶναι ἀμείνων.
sentences.tr:
hōi ou tis toi erizetai enthade g’ anēr,
oude tis en Lykiēi seo g’ euchetai einai ameinōn.
sentences.l:
In which no man here at least vies with you,
nor does anyone in Lycia claim to be better than you.
sentences.i: In that no man here rivals you, nor does anyone in Lycia claim to be better than you.
sentences.n: ᾧ ‘in which’ (a relative in the dative of respect) looks back to what has just been named, most naturally κλέος ‘fame’: ‘in which no man here rivals you’. ἐρίζεται is ‘rivals, vies’ and ἐνθάδε γ’ ‘here, at least’. In the second half οὐδέ τις ‘nor anyone’ is the subject of εὔχεται εἶναι ‘claims to be’, with the comparative ἀμείνων ‘better’ and σέο γ’ (= σοῦ γε) ‘than you’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε τῷδ’ ἔφες ἀνδρὶ βέλος Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχὼν
ὅς τις ὅδε κρατέει καὶ δὴ κακὰ πολλὰ ἔοργε
Τρῶας, ἐπεὶ πολλῶν τε καὶ ἐσθλῶν γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ age tōid’ ephes andri belos Dii cheiras anaschōn
hos tis hode krateei kai dē kaka polla eorge
Trōas, epei pollōn te kai esthlōn gounat’ elysen·
sentences.i: But come, shoot a shaft at this man, raising your hands to Zeus — whoever he is who is prevailing and has already done the Trojans many evils, since he has loosed the knees of many good men;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’. ἔφες is the aorist imperative of ἐφίημι ‘shoot at, send at’, with βέλος ‘shaft’ as object and τῷδ’ ἀνδρί ‘this man’ in the dative. Διὶ χεῖρας ἀνασχών ‘raising your hands to Zeus’ is the gesture of prayer: the shot is to be made with a prayer. ὅς τις ὅδε is ‘whoever this man is who’, κρατέει ‘prevails’, and δὴ … ἔοργε is ‘has already done’ (ἔοργε the perfect of ἔρδω ‘do’), with κακὰ πολλά ‘many evils’ and Τρῶας ‘to the Trojans’. γούνατ’ ἔλυσεν ‘loosed the knees’ is the idiom for killing, and ἐσθλῶν ‘good’ means brave.

sentences.t:
εἰ μή τις θεός ἐστι κοτεσσάμενος Τρώεσσιν
ἱρῶν μηνίσας· χαλεπὴ δὲ θεοῦ ἔπι μῆνις.
sentences.tr:
ei mē tis theos esti kotessamenos Trōessin
hirōn mēnisas· chalepē de theou epi mēnis.
sentences.l:
unless it is some god, bearing a grudge against the Trojans,
wrathful over sacrifices; hard is a god’s wrath when it is upon one.”
sentences.i: unless it is some god who bears a grudge against the Trojans, wrathful over sacrifices; for hard is the wrath of a god when it is upon one.”
sentences.n: εἰ μή is ‘unless’. τις θεός ἐστι κοτεσσάμενος is ‘some god is bearing a grudge’ (κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, the aorist participle, with the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘against the Trojans’), and ἱρῶν μηνίσας is ‘angry over sacrifices’: μηνίσας is the aorist participle of μηνίω ‘be wrathful’, the verb of μῆνις ‘wrath’, and the genitive ἱρῶν gives the cause (the Greek does not say whose sacrifices or how they failed). χαλεπὴ δὲ θεοῦ ἔπι μῆνις is a saying, ‘and hard is the wrath of a god when it is upon one’; ἔπι here is either ἔπεστι ‘is upon’ or the preposition set after its noun. Aeneas’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Lykaonos aglaos huios·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Lycaon’s splendid son:
sentences.i: Then Lycaon’s splendid son spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the stock introduction of a reply, ‘and to him in turn he spoke’; προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’. Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Lycaon’s splendid son’ is Pandarus, named by his father (ἀγλαός ‘splendid’).

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία Τρώων βουληφόρε χαλκοχιτώνων
Τυδεΐδῃ μιν ἔγωγε δαΐφρονι πάντα ἐΐσκω,
sentences.tr:
Aineia Trōōn boulēphore chalkochitōnōn
Tydeïdēi min egōge daïphroni panta eïskō,
sentences.l:
“Aeneas, counsel-bearer of the bronze-shirted Trojans,
to the wise-minded son of Tydeus him I, for my part, liken in everything,
sentences.i: “Aeneas, counsellor of the bronze-shirted Trojans, I for my part liken him in everything to the wise-hearted son of Tydeus,
sentences.n: Αἰνεία is the vocative of Αἰνείας, and βουληφόρε the vocative of βουληφόρος, ‘counsel-bearing’, ‘counsellor’, with Τρώων χαλκοχιτώνων ‘of the bronze-shirted Trojans’. Τυδεΐδῃ … δαΐφρονι ‘to the wise-minded son of Tydeus’ is dative with ἐΐσκω ‘I liken’; μιν is ‘him’, the man they are both watching, ἔγωγε ‘I for my part’, and πάντα ‘in everything’. The sense of δαΐφρων (‘wise’ or ‘fierce’) is disputed; ‘wise-minded’ is the usual choice.

sentences.t:
ἀσπίδι γιγνώσκων αὐλώπιδί τε τρυφαλείῃ,
ἵππους τ’ εἰσορόων·
sentences.tr:
aspidi gignōskōn aulōpidi te tryphaleiēi,
hippous t’ eisoroōn·
sentences.l:
recognising him by his shield and tubed helm,
and looking at the horses;
sentences.i: recognising him by his shield and tubed helmet, and by the sight of the horses;
sentences.n: ἀσπίδι … γιγνώσκων is ‘recognising him by his shield’ (dative of means) and αὐλώπιδι … τρυφαλείῃ ‘by his tubed helm’: the sense of αὐλῶπις is not known, and it is usually explained from αὐλός ‘tube’ as having a socket for the plume. ἵππους τ’ εἰσορόων is ‘and looking at the horses’ (εἰσοράω, the present participle in -όων for -ῶν).

sentences.t: σάφα δ’ οὐκ οἶδ’ εἰ θεός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr: sapha d’ ouk oid’ ei theos estin.
sentences.l: but clearly I do not know whether he is a god.
sentences.i: but I cannot say for certain whether he is a god.
sentences.n: σάφα ‘clearly, for certain’ is an adverb with οὐκ οἶδ’ (οἶδα ‘I know’), and εἰ θεός ἐστιν is the indirect question ‘whether he is a god’. Pandarus can recognise the man’s gear but cannot tell whether a god is with him; the next lines give both possibilities.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὅ γ’ ἀνὴρ ὅν φημι δαΐφρων Τυδέος υἱὸς
οὐχ ὅ γ’ ἄνευθε θεοῦ τάδε μαίνεται,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ ho g’ anēr hon phēmi daïphrōn Tydeos huios
ouch ho g’ aneuthe theou tade mainetai,
sentences.l:
But if he is the man I say, the wise-minded son of Tydeus,
not without a god does he rage in this way,
sentences.i: But if he is the man I say he is, the wise-hearted son of Tydeus, he does not rage like this without a god,
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ὅ γ’ ἀνήρ ὅν φημι … is ‘but if he is the man I say’: ὅν is the relative ‘whom’, and δαΐφρων Τυδέος υἱός stands in apposition. The main clause is οὐχ ὅ γ’ ἄνευθε θεοῦ τάδε μαίνεται, ‘he does not rage like this without a god’: ἄνευθε takes the genitive θεοῦ, μαίνεται is ‘rages’ (μαίνομαι), and τάδε is ‘in this way’. The sentence goes on into the next unit with ἀλλά.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τις ἄγχι
ἕστηκ’ ἀθανάτων νεφέλῃ εἰλυμένος ὤμους,
ὃς τούτου βέλος ὠκὺ κιχήμενον ἔτραπεν ἄλλῃ.
sentences.tr:
alla tis anchi
hestēk’ athanatōn nephelēi eilymenos ōmous,
hos toutou belos ōky kichēmenon etrapen allēi.
sentences.l:
but some one stands near, of the immortals,
wrapped about the shoulders in cloud,
who turned elsewhere the swift shaft as it was reaching this man.
sentences.i: but one of the immortals stands near, his shoulders wrapped in cloud, who turned aside the swift shaft as it was reaching him.
sentences.n: ἀλλά τις ἄγχι ἕστηκ’ is ‘but someone stands near’: ἕστηκ’ is ἕστηκε, the perfect of ἵστημι, used as a present ‘stands’, and ἀθανάτων ‘of the immortals’ goes with τις. νεφέλῃ εἰλυμένος ὤμους is ‘wrapped in cloud as to the shoulders’ (εἰλυμένος the perfect passive participle of εἰλύω ‘wrap’, ὤμους the accusative of the part wrapped). ὃς … ἔτραπεν ἄλλῃ is ‘who turned aside’ (ἔτραπεν the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’, ἄλλῃ ‘another way’). Its object is βέλος ὠκὺ κιχήμενον, ‘the swift shaft as it was reaching’ (κιχήμενον is an epic form of the participle of κιχάνω ‘reach’); τούτου ‘this man’ stands before the shaft and is taken as the genitive after κιχήμενον, ‘reaching this man’. The construction is loose, and the sense is the shaft that was reaching him.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ οἱ ἐφῆκα βέλος, καί μιν βάλον ὦμον
δεξιὸν ἀντικρὺ διὰ θώρηκος γυάλοιο·
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar hoi ephēka belos, kai min balon ōmon
dexion antikry dia thōrēkos gyaloio·
sentences.l:
For already at him I shot a shaft, and him I struck on the shoulder,
the right one, straight on through the hollow breastplate;
sentences.i: I have already shot a shaft at him, and hit him on the right shoulder, right through the hollow breastplate;
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ gives the proof: ‘for already’. ἐφῆκα is the aorist of ἐφίημι, ‘I shot at’, with οἱ ‘at him’ (dative) and βέλος ‘a shaft’; καί μιν βάλον ὦμον δεξιόν is ‘and I hit him on the right shoulder’ (the shoulder in the accusative, as the part struck). ἀντικρύ ‘straight on, right through’ goes with διὰ θώρηκος γυάλοιο, ‘through the hollow breastplate’ (γυάλοιο agrees with θώρηκος; at 5.99 the same word, γύαλον, is a noun for the hollow of the plate). This is the shot Pandarus made at 5.98–99.

sentences.t:
καί μιν ἔγωγ’ ἐφάμην Ἀϊδωνῆϊ προϊάψειν,
ἔμπης δ’ οὐκ ἐδάμασσα· θεός νύ τίς ἐστι κοτήεις.
sentences.tr:
kai min egōg’ ephamēn Aïdōnēï proïapsein,
empēs d’ ouk edamassa· theos ny tis esti kotēeis.
sentences.l:
and him I for my part said I would send-forth to Aidoneus,
but all the same I did not subdue him; a god, then, is he, some resentful one.
sentences.i: and I thought I would fling him down to Aidoneus, yet I did not overcome him; so there is some resentful god.
sentences.n: καί μιν ἔγωγ’ ἐφάμην … προϊάψειν is ‘and I said I would send him’: ἐφάμην is the imperfect of φημί, with the future infinitive προϊάψειν ‘to send forth, fling down’, to Ἀϊδωνῆϊ, the dative of Ἀϊδωνεύς ‘Aidoneus’, another name for Hades. ἔμπης δ’ is ‘but all the same’, οὐκ ἐδάμασσα ‘I did not subdue him’ (δαμάζω), and θεός νύ τίς ἐστι κοτήεις is ‘so some resentful god it is’: κοτήεις ‘resentful’ comes from κότος ‘resentment’, and νύ ‘then’ marks the inference.

sentences.t: ἵπποι δ’ οὐ παρέασι καὶ ἅρματα τῶν κ’ ἐπιβαίην·
sentences.tr: hippoi d’ ou pareasi kai harmata tōn k’ epibaiēn·
sentences.l: and horses are not here, nor chariots, of which I might mount;
sentences.i: but there are no horses or chariots here that I could mount;
sentences.n: ἵπποι δ’ οὐ παρέασι καὶ ἅρματα is ‘but horses are not present, and chariots’: παρέασι is πάρεισι ‘are present’, and the ‘not’ covers both nouns. The relative clause τῶν κ’ ἐπιβαίην is ‘which I might mount’: ἐπιβαίνω takes the genitive, and κ’ (= κε) with the optative ἐπιβαίην makes it potential. Pandarus is explaining why he is on foot.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά που ἐν μεγάροισι Λυκάονος ἕνδεκα δίφροι
καλοὶ πρωτοπαγεῖς νεοτευχέες·
sentences.tr:
alla pou en megaroisi Lykaonos hendeka diphroi
kaloi prōtopageis neoteuchees·
sentences.l:
but doubtless in the halls of Lycaon eleven chariots,
fine, newly built, freshly made;
sentences.i: But in Lycaon’s halls there are doubtless eleven chariots, fine ones, newly built and freshly made;
sentences.n: ἀλλά που is ‘but, no doubt’; που softens the claim. Λυκάονος is Pandarus’ father, and ἐν μεγάροισι ‘in the halls’. ἕνδεκα δίφροι ‘eleven chariots’ is the subject with the verb ‘are’ left out; καλοί ‘fine’ is followed by two compounds, πρωτοπαγεῖς ‘newly built’ (from πρῶτος ‘first’ and πήγνυμι ‘fix’) and νεοτευχέες ‘freshly made’ (from νέος ‘new’ and τεύχω ‘make’).

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ πέπλοι
πέπτανται· παρὰ δέ σφιν ἑκάστῳ δίζυγες ἵπποι
ἑστᾶσι κρῖ λευκὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι καὶ ὀλύρας.
sentences.tr:
amphi de peploi
peptantai· para de sphin hekastōi dizyges hippoi
hestasi kri leukon ereptomenoi kai olyras.
sentences.l:
and around them cloths
have been spread; and beside each of them paired horses
stand, feeding on white barley and spelt.
sentences.i: Cloths are spread around them, and beside each one stand paired horses, feeding on white barley and spelt.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δὲ πέπλοι πέπτανται: πέπλοι (‘robes, cloths’) are here covers spread around the chariots, and πέπτανται is the perfect passive of πετάννυμι ‘spread out’. παρὰ δέ σφιν ἑκάστῳ is ‘and beside each of them’ (σφιν = the chariots), δίζυγες ἵπποι ‘paired horses’ (δίζυξ ‘yoked in twos’), and ἑστᾶσι ‘they stand’ (the perfect of ἵστημι). κρῖ λευκόν ‘white barley’ and ὀλύρας (the accusative plural of ὀλύρα, a kind of grain, usually guessed to be spelt) are what ἐρεπτόμενοι ‘feeding on’ takes.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μοι μάλα πολλὰ γέρων αἰχμητὰ Λυκάων
ἐρχομένῳ ἐπέτελλε δόμοις ἔνι ποιητοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
ē men moi mala polla gerōn aichmēta Lykaōn
erchomenōi epetelle domois eni poiētoisin·
sentences.l:
Truly, very many things the old spearman Lycaon
enjoined on me as I set out, in his well-made house;
sentences.i: Truly, old Lycaon the spearman gave me many instructions as I was setting out, in his well-built house;
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly’. γέρων αἰχμητὰ Λυκάων is ‘old Lycaon the spearman’ (αἰχμητά is a nominative in -α, like ἱππότα; the word comes from αἰχμή ‘spear-point’). μάλα πολλά ‘very many things’ is the object of ἐπέτελλε ‘he enjoined’ (the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω), and ἐρχομένῳ is ‘to me as I set out’ (a dative participle). δόμοις ἔνι ποιητοῖσιν is ‘in the well-made house’: ἔνι is ἐν set after its noun, and the plural δόμοις is a poetic plural.

sentences.t:
ἵπποισίν μ’ ἐκέλευε καὶ ἅρμασιν ἐμβεβαῶτα
ἀρχεύειν Τρώεσσι κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας·
sentences.tr:
hippoisin m’ ekeleue kai harmasin embebaōta
archeuein Trōessi kata krateras hysminas·
sentences.l:
he urged me, mounted on horses and chariot,
to lead the Trojans through the strong battles;
sentences.i: he told me to mount horses and chariot and lead the Trojans through the strong battles;
sentences.n: ἐκέλευε ‘urged, told’ has μ’ (με) as its object, with ἐμβεβαῶτα the perfect participle of ἐμβαίνω, ‘having mounted’, standing on ἵπποισιν καὶ ἅρμασιν ‘horses and chariot’. ἀρχεύειν Τρώεσσι is ‘to be leader of the Trojans’, and κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας is ‘through the strong battles’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ οὐ πιθόμην· ἦ τ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν·
ἵππων φειδόμενος, μή μοι δευοίατο φορβῆς
ἀνδρῶν εἰλομένων εἰωθότες ἔδμεναι ἄδην.
sentences.tr:
all’ egō ou pithomēn· ē t’ an poly kerdion ēen·
hippōn pheidomenos, mē moi deuoiato phorbēs
andrōn eilomenōn eiōthotes edmenai adēn.
sentences.l:
But I did not obey, — truly much better it would have been, —
sparing the horses, lest for me they should lack fodder,
with men being crowded together, they accustomed to eat their fill.
sentences.i: But I did not obey — and it would surely have been far better if I had — because I was sparing my horses, afraid that, with men crowded together, they would lack fodder, they who were used to eating their fill.
sentences.n: πιθόμην is the aorist middle of πείθω, ‘I obeyed’. ἦ τ’ ἂν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν is ‘it would truly have been much better’: ἦεν is ἦν, and the comparative κέρδιον is ‘better’ (the first line also stands in the Odyssey). ἵππων φειδόμενος ‘sparing the horses’ (φείδομαι takes the genitive) gives his reason; μή … δευοίατο φορβῆς is ‘lest they lack fodder’ (the optative of δεύομαι ‘lack’ with the genitive), ἀνδρῶν εἰλομένων is a genitive absolute, ‘men being crowded together’ (εἴλομαι), and εἰωθότες ἔδμεναι ἄδην is ‘used to eating their fill’ (the perfect participle of ἔθω, the infinitive ἔδμεναι ‘to eat’, ἄδην ‘to satiety’).

sentences.t:
ὣς λίπον, αὐτὰρ πεζὸς ἐς Ἴλιον εἰλήλουθα
τόξοισιν πίσυνος· τὰ δέ μ’ οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ὀνήσειν.
sentences.tr:
hōs lipon, autar pezos es Ilion eilēloutha
toxoisin pisynos· ta de m’ ouk ar’ emellon onēsein.
sentences.l:
So I left them, but on foot to Ilios I have come,
trusting in my bow; but it was not, as it turned out, going to profit me.
sentences.i: So I left them, and have come to Ilios on foot, trusting in my bow; but it was not, as it turned out, going to do me any good.
sentences.n: ὣς λίπον is ‘so I left (them)’, that is the horses and chariots. πεζός ‘on foot’, ἐς Ἴλιον εἰλήλουθα ‘I have come to Ilios’ (the perfect of ἔρχομαι), and τόξοισιν πίσυνος ‘trusting in my bow’ (the plural τόξα stands for a single bow, as often; πίσυνος takes the dative). τὰ δέ is ‘but this’, the bow picked up again as a plural, and οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ὀνήσειν is ‘was not, as it turned out, going to profit’: ἔμελλον with the future infinitive of ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’, ἄρα ‘so it proved’, and μ’ ‘me’.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ δοιοῖσιν ἀριστήεσσιν ἐφῆκα
Τυδεΐδῃ τε καὶ Ἀτρεΐδῃ,
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar doioisin aristēessin ephēka
Tydeïdēi te kai Atreïdēi,
sentences.l:
For already at two best men I shot,
at the son of Tydeus and the son of Atreus,
sentences.i: I have already shot at two of the best men, the son of Tydeus and the son of Atreus,
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ ‘for already’ brings a second proof. ἐφῆκα is ‘I shot at’ (the dative again, with the shaft left unsaid), and δοιοῖσιν ἀριστήεσσιν is ‘two best men’ (δοιός ‘two’, ἀριστῆες ‘the best’). Τυδεΐδῃ and Ἀτρεΐδῃ are patronymics in the dative; Ἀτρεΐδῃ is Menelaus here, whom Pandarus wounded in Book 4, though the Greek gives only the patronymic.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἀμφοτέροιιν
ἀτρεκὲς αἷμ’ ἔσσευα βαλών, ἤγειρα δὲ μᾶλλον.
sentences.tr:
ek d’ amphoteroiin
atrekes haim’ esseua balōn, ēgeira de mallon.
sentences.l:
and from both
truly blood I made rush, having hit them, but I roused them the more.
sentences.i: and from both I made the blood run, truly, when I hit them, but I only roused them the more.
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἀμφοτέροιιν is ‘from both’ (ἀμφοτέροιιν is the dual genitive), ἀτρεκές ‘truly’ (an adverb from the same family as ἀτρεκέως ‘exactly’; the exact force is not settled), αἷμ’ ἔσσευα ‘I made the blood rush’ (ἔσσευα the aorist of σεύω ‘set in motion’), and βαλών ‘having hit’. ἤγειρα δὲ μᾶλλον is ‘but I roused them the more’ (ἤγειρα from ἐγείρω ‘rouse’): the wounds only stirred them up.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥα κακῇ αἴσῃ ἀπὸ πασσάλου ἀγκύλα τόξα
ἤματι τῷ ἑλόμην ὅτε Ἴλιον εἰς ἐρατεινὴν
ἡγεόμην Τρώεσσι φέρων χάριν Ἕκτορι δίῳ.
sentences.tr:
tō rha kakēi aisēi apo passalou ankyla toxa
ēmati tōi helomēn hote Ilion eis erateinēn
hēgeomēn Trōessi pherōn charin Hektori diōi.
sentences.l:
So then, with an evil portion, from the peg the curved bow
on that day I took, when to lovely Ilios
I led the Trojans, bringing a favour to heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: So it was with an evil lot that I took the curved bow down from its peg on the day I led the Trojans to lovely Ilios, bringing a favour to heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: τώ ῥα ‘so then’ (τώ ‘therefore’) says that taking up the bow was a mistake. κακῇ αἴσῃ is ‘with an evil lot’; ἀπὸ πασσάλου is ‘from the peg’ on which the bow hung; ἀγκύλα τόξα is ‘the curved bow’ (a plural for one bow); and ἑλόμην is the aorist middle of αἱρέω. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on the day when’ (ἦμαρ ‘day’), Ἴλιον εἰς ἐρατεινήν ‘to lovely Ilios’, ἡγεόμην Τρώεσσι ‘I led the Trojans’ (ἡγέομαι takes the dative), and φέρων χάριν Ἕκτορι δίῳ ‘bringing a favour to heavenly Hector’: he went to oblige Hector.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε νοστήσω καὶ ἐσόψομαι ὀφθαλμοῖσι
πατρίδ’ ἐμὴν ἄλοχόν τε καὶ ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα,
sentences.tr:
ei de ke nostēsō kai esopsomai ophthalmoisi
patrid’ emēn alochon te kai hypserephes mega dōma,
sentences.l:
But if I return home and see with my eyes
my fatherland and my wife and my high-roofed great house,
sentences.i: But if I return home and see with my own eyes my fatherland and my wife and my great high-roofed house,
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κε νοστήσω is ‘but if I come home’: εἰ with κε and the aorist subjunctive. ἐσόψομαι is the future of εἰσοράω ‘I shall see’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσι ‘with my eyes’. The three things he will see are πατρίδ’ ἐμήν ‘my fatherland’, ἄλοχον ‘wife’, and ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα ‘my great high-roofed house’ (ὑψερεφής, from ὑψί ‘high’ and ἐρέφω ‘roof’).

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπ’ ἐμεῖο κάρη τάμοι ἀλλότριος φὼς
εἰ μὴ ἐγὼ τάδε τόξα φαεινῷ ἐν πυρὶ θείην
χερσὶ διακλάσσας·
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeit’ ap’ emeio karē tamoi allotrios phōs
ei mē egō tade toxa phaeinōi en pyri theiēn
chersi diaklassas·
sentences.i: then may a foreign man cut my head from me at once, if I do not put this bow in the shining fire, breaking it to pieces with my hands;
sentences.n: αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ‘at once then’ begins the result of the oath. The optative τάμοι (the aorist of τέμνω ‘cut’) is a wish, ‘may … cut off’, with the subject ἀλλότριος φώς ‘a foreign man’ (φώς is ‘man’, ἀλλότριος ‘belonging to another, foreign’), the object κάρη ‘head’, and ἀπ’ ἐμεῖο ‘from me’ (epic genitive). εἰ μή … θείην is ‘if I do not put’ (the aorist optative of τίθημι), τάδε τόξα is ‘this bow’, φαεινῷ ἐν πυρί ‘in the shining fire’, and χερσὶ διακλάσσας ‘breaking it to pieces with my hands’ (the aorist participle of διακλάω).

sentences.t: ἀνεμώλια γάρ μοι ὀπηδεῖ.
sentences.tr: anemōlia gar moi opēdei.
sentences.l: for emptily it attends me.”
sentences.i: for it keeps company with me to no purpose.”
sentences.n: ἀνεμώλια is a neuter plural adjective used like an adverb, ‘emptily, to no purpose’ (ἀνεμώλιος ‘empty’, from ἄνεμος ‘wind’, as in ἀνεμώλια βάζεις); γάρ gives the reason for breaking the bow, and ὀπηδεῖ is ‘attends, follows’ (ὀπηδέω), with μοι ‘me’. Pandarus’ speech ends here.
